title: Understanding Unit Economics
summary: Learn how much money a business earns or loses from one sale.

chapters.title: What is unit economics?
chapters.description: Unit economics tells us how much money a business earns or loses by selling one unit. See what a unit is for eight common businesses.

blocks.heading: What it means
blocks.text: Unit economics tells us how much money a business earns or loses by selling one unit.
A unit is one thing a customer buys from you. It can be one order, one appointment or one monthly plan.

blocks.heading: The main question
blocks.text: When we acquire one more customer, do we earn enough money to cover the cost of acquiring and serving that customer?
Acquiring a customer means getting them to buy, for example through ads. Serving them means delivering what they paid for.

blocks.heading: What a unit looks like
blocks.caption: The unit is different for every business.

chapters.takeaway: A unit is whatever one customer buys from you. Pick the unit first, then count money per unit.

chapters.title: The profit per unit formula
chapters.description: Profit per unit is revenue per unit minus cost per unit. Learn the formula and try it on five real business examples with the calculator.

blocks.heading: Revenue and cost
items: Revenue is the money received from one sale.
Cost is the money spent to acquire and serve that customer.

blocks.heading: The formula
blocks.text: Profit per unit = Revenue per unit − Cost per unit
blocks.note: If the answer is below zero, the business loses money on every sale.

blocks.heading: Try the calculator
blocks.intro: Pick a business. Then change the price or any cost and watch the profit change.

chapters.takeaway: Profit per unit is what is left of one sale after every cost of that sale.

chapters.title: What counts as cost
chapters.description: Count every rupee spent because of one sale: ads, commission, materials, packaging, delivery, staff time, payment charges and support.

blocks.heading: Count everything spent on one sale
blocks.text: Count everything you spend because of that one sale. If the sale did not happen, you would not spend this money.

blocks.heading: Examples of each cost
rows: Instagram ads that brought in the customer
A 20% cut paid to a food delivery app
Flour, sugar and cream for one cake
The box and bag for one order
The courier fee for one parcel
The stylist's pay for one haircut
The 2% fee on a UPI or card payment
Time spent answering one customer's calls

blocks.title: Not counted here
blocks.text: Fixed expenses like rent, electricity and permanent salaries are not counted here. They come in Module 2.

chapters.takeaway: Count every cost that one sale creates. Leave fixed expenses like rent for later.

chapters.title: Good units and poor units
chapters.description: A profitable unit grows profit with every sale. A loss-making unit grows the loss. See why more sales do not always mean more profit.

blocks.heading: Two kinds of units
blocks.caption: Same price, different costs. Look at what happens after 1,000 sales.

blocks.text: The loss-making business sold just as many units. It still lost ₹2,00,000, because every sale cost more than it earned.

blocks.heading: Revenue is not profit
blocks.text: More sales do not always mean more profit. Revenue is the money that comes in. Profit is what stays with you after costs.
Take the clothing brand from Chapter 2. It sells a shirt for ₹1,200, but only ₹200 is left after all costs.

chapters.takeaway: Check profit per unit before you spend more on ads. Ads on a loss-making unit only grow the loss.

chapters.title: Worked examples
chapters.description: Profit per unit worked out for a restaurant, a salon, an online course, a clothing brand and a bakery, with full cost tables.

blocks.heading: Five businesses
blocks.intro: Pick a business to see its cost table and result.

blocks.heading: What the numbers show
blocks.text: All five businesses make a profit on each unit, but the amount is very different. The online course keeps ₹700 of ₹2,000. The shirt keeps only ₹200 of ₹1,200.

chapters.takeaway: The formula is the same for every business. The costs are what make one unit strong and another weak.

chapters.title: Practice assignment
chapters.description: Work out the unit, revenue, cost and profit for a bakery selling birthday cakes. Check your answers to complete the module.

blocks.heading: The problem
blocks.text: A bakery sells one birthday cake for ₹1,500. These are its costs for one cake.

blocks.heading: Questions
items: What is the revenue per unit?
What is the total cost per unit?
What is the profit per unit?
What is the profit from 30 cakes?

blocks.heading: Check your answers
blocks.intro: Enter numbers only. Get all three right to complete this chapter.

chapters.takeaway: Pick the unit, add up every cost of one sale and take it away from the price. What is left is your profit per unit.
